entry.title: about me
entry.content:
this entry has been edited, and probably will continue to be edited, since its initial post-date

Hello! My name is Julia, and I am a recent graduate from the University of Chicago, currently based in Hyde Park. Broadly, I am interested in reconstructing paleoecologies through time, using quantitative and comparative approaches to examine organisms as a part of larger ecological and evolutionary systems. Alongside paleontological research, I also developing a background in scientific illustration and paleoart.

Interested in paleontology and planetary science, I majored in Geophysical Sciences with a minor in Astrophysicas. I tend to understand Earth history as a dynamic biogeochemical system shaped by evolution, extinction, and origination over time across time. Much of my current work grows out of that perspective, combining computational and creative approaches to better understand how organisms and ecosystems changed – and, particularly, how that reconstruction can be done from incomplete records and imitated established frameworks.

My recent research has focused on pterosaur phylogeny, mammalian herbivory, and methodological questions around ecological and evolutionary inference. Using approaches ranging from Bayesian phylogenetics to multivariate ecological modeling, I am particularly interested in investigating convergence, long-term vertebrate evolutionary patterns, ecosystem recoveries, and the relationship between the reality of the past and the systems we use to represent it. By exploring different organizational approaches to data, I hope to leverage their strengths against their weaknesses to reveal otherwise hidden signal.

Alongside research, I use writing and visual art to explore paleontology and reconstruction from a more personal and interpretive perspective. I am interested in how scientific models, images, and narratives shape our understanding of (past and present) life and humanity’s position within it. My artwork is both a means of improving my understanding (through anatomy, research, and reconstruction) and a means to ‘bring to life’ a past long-gone.

Outside of my research and art, I am interested in the philosophy of science, visualizing the past, and (very unrelatedly) religious syncretism in antiquity. I also enjoy gardening, rockclimbing, and concerts

entry.title: GitHub GitVent
entry.content:
I began working on this site in August 2025, and always thought it was taxing. I had it set up to work with in VScode, synced to GitHub. I made my edits, then waited patiently for the deploy workflow to run, checked it out, made more edits.

Notice anything?

I completely forgot and/or did not know in this usecase one could run local builds for testing site features.

My head aches at the thought of all the time wasted for the 5 min sync and deploy cycles, cycles that put me off editing the site and left it in development hell for months as I found focus on other things.

Mistakes must be made to learn, but this one was certainly cringe-worthy.

entry.title: returning
entry.content:
If you’ve come across this site before (or, more likely, you’ve spotted the publish date on the last post), you may have noticed that there hasn’t been an update in some time. Counterintuitively, its not for a lack of ideas – I’ve had lists and lists of jotted down brain-dump ideas and prompts recorded in my back-pocket journal at work. The problem has been twofold: the starting, and the quality.

While I come up with ideas, I never seem to sit down and write…if there’s anything I’ve now learned about post-college life, it is that it’s a constant cycle: dishes, cooking, laundry…Sisyphus, I imagine, did not need to spend so much time exchanging cash for quarters (a coin-only machine in my 2026?!). There’s too much time and never-enough for all the projects I want to complete – all the things I should do but equally am prohibited from beginning … some reason or another take priority over creative work.

I used to write quite often. My digital sticky-notes filled with my seminar thoughts, notes between classes, and tasks; essay-outlines, rambles, and rants would fill 50 pages of a word doc, and crash the Sticky Notes program. I’ve had 10 paper journals or so since ~the start of the Covid pandemic. But I was a STEM major in university - writing became code comments, lab reports, and networking emails. I didn’t read as often. My friends graduated, or moved off campus. Conversations and practice articulating my thoughts faded to the back-burner in lieu of PSets and Reddit to pass the time. Getting back into the habit has been…more difficult than I thought it would be. It feels like riding a bike after years and finding yoursel falling - its not supposed to be something that you can forget.

I am a creative – I, nominally, am used to the hardship of the process. Its supposed to be challenging! But in academics, there are ‘rules.’ There are explicit styles for scientific writing; lab reports are a genre. In a 8-10 week quarter, why not use something that helps move things along more quickly? Something trained to be an expert in those very standards? In a fast-paced environment, why not reach for the tool that, nominally, can quickly evaluate your work with a body of human knowledge behind it? ChatGPT, and any of these new LLMs, feel like a drug. Steroids. A quick-fix and quick-soluton to ever intense incentives. There are practical uses - I’ve been able to explore data in ways I never could before - but in writing? I feel my work being homogenized. I tell it to point out flaws, and lose the ability to recognize them myself. Suddenly, everything I create is getting passed through its computerized-filter. Composed to promote engagement, there is always some identified flaw, always something wrong, always some polite suggestion. It wants to turn my paragraphs into its own style. A corporate style. A style with wide appeal. My own style, my own writing ability, atrophies – and when I open my laptop, I feel the urge to pull up a tab for ChatGPT. “The Great Averager” is and has always been an apt name.

Any kind of writing for me, these days, is personal. Existential topics churning in the back of my mind bleed into whatever post, essay, or journal entry I start. Efforts to say something poignant about some particular issue expand in scope until its too much for a single work, and too unfocused for anything other than a diary. In many ways, I’ve forgotten how to start, and I’ve forgotten how to edit. But, and maybe this is the worst thing that LLMs have done to me, despite holding off for so long, despite hopping on the bandwagon so late, is that I am beginning to lose confidence in my abilities. To no longer trust my own writing, or my ideas. ChatGPT can always come up with something better – my voice more clear through its text than my own writing. I can feel that fear constant in my mind, despite the work I produce. The dependency encouraged and projected onto a software that portends to be our culture’s magnum opus. As a scientist, I risk losing what makes my perspective distinct. As an individual, I risk losing the abilities I once held dear.

I want to write - I want to add my opinions to the pile. I have takes! I have ideas! I just…need to do it, like most other things in my life. I want to recover from the brain-rot AI social media atrophy of abilities, recover from this … modern deal with the devil.

I went to the University of Chicago. Are we not known for being a bit quirky? In the coming weeks, I hope to rekindle that side of my work. My writing will not hold back from being too personal, but nor will it avoid the intersection of science and the experience of being a scientist - embedded in social issues and political crises. I will write about post-college experiences. How I organize information to retain autonomy over my collections. The despair I feel reading the news - and how I avoid doomerism. What my goals are. What I have accomplished. And how I am moving forward.

Enjoy, Julia.

entry.title: launching ‘off the fossil record’
entry.content:
Welcome!

Hi! AS I’ve said in the “about me” post, my name is Julia, a semi-recent graduate from the University of Chicago. I was a geoscience major interested in paleontology, planetary science, and earth history - I also spent time on art and an amateur interest in religious history.

This site exists for two primary reasons: for one, to document my academic projects, but also, to host my writing and science-related artwork. By recording about academic topics outside the context of papers or reports, I hope to deepen my understanding of my areas of interest – and by hosting a website, I hope to gather materials into consolidated pages not just for my own use, but also for my fellows researchers. In my writing, I plan to discuss recent publications, artwork, current events, and my own experiences as a first-gen woman in academia. Inspired by Astrobites & 7DaysofScience, that may mean anything from musings on the way we represent evolution, to entries on UChicago specifically, to responses to pop-science essays. Generally, grappling with the role paleontology has in our daily lives, society, and my own academic trajectory. If you’re interested in bigger questions – how we define evolutionary “success,” where we fit on the tree of life, and how we feel about those relationships – that will likely be here, too.

Oh - and occasionally I’ll air my grievances about obscure papers or fawn over the newest discoveries on niche clades (with a special fondness for Nyctosauridae and Anurognathidae, both pterosaurs, and some mammalian lineages).
